# Running example — 영상 3개로 추적하는 보고서 생성 파이프라인 (통합본)

- 장(##)·절(###)·하위 절(####)을 문서 순서대로 모두 실었다. 제목을 누르면 그 위치로 간다.
- 〔 〕 안의 숫자는 그 절 본문(하위 절 제외)에 있는 표·그림·접힌 원문(`<details>`)의 개수다. 접힌 원문은 눌러야 펼쳐진다.
- §2–§5와 §7은 세 영상을 나란히 비교하고, §6은 영상별로 섹션 6개를 따라간다. §10은 농구 영상(`-QuCz7kxBr8`) 한 건의 심층 자료다.

## 0. 문서 안내

- **목적**: 프레임워크의 구조·모듈 동작·중간 산출물을 보여 주는 발표 자료의 근거 문서다. 같은 질의·같은 설정으로 만든 보고서 3건(영상별 r1)이 입력 → 오프라인 메모리 → 실행 준비 → planner → 섹션별 query·검색·writer·후처리 → 최종 산출물·검증을 거치는 동안의 **실제 입력과 출력**을 단계별로 보여 준다.
- **구성**
  - §2–§5와 §7은 단계별로 세 영상을 나란히 둔다.
  - §6(섹션별 처리)은 영상별로 섹션 6개를 모두 따라간다.
  - §8은 단계별 문제점·한계, §9는 재생성 방법과 발표 활용이다.
  - §10은 발표 예시 영상 `-QuCz7kxBr8`(농구) 한 건의 심층 자료다: 사전 구축 메모리(캡션 계층·OpenIE·그래프·semantic·visual)의 실제 내용, 캡션·임베딩 모델이 받은 프레임 그림, 섹션별 모든 모듈의 입력·출력 원문과 검색 내부 과정(CPU 재현).
- **대상**: `outputs/p9p19_check_20261025_141401/<영상>__c0_written__r1/` 3건. 2026-10-25 실행, 커밋 `baf08d8` 시점 코드. 2026-10-26 변경(영상 끝 근거 txt0, 반복 경고 기준, 결말 검사 오탐 수정)은 들어 있지 않고 GPU 확인 전이다.
- **만든 방법** (재생성 가능, GPU 불필요, LLM 재호출 없음)
  - 사실 부분: `analysis/build_running_example_combined.py`가 기록 파일에서 직접 생성했다.
    - Deep-Reporter 세션 로그(planner·query·writer 프롬프트와 출력 원문)
    - `report.json`·`validation.json`·`report.md`
    - LLM 서버·검색 서비스 로그
    - WorldMM 캡션·semantic·visual 파일, HippoRAG 캐시, Video-MME 메타, 영상 파일
  - 생성할 때 자동으로 확인한 것
    - 후처리기를 `report.json`에 다시 돌린 결과가 `report.md`와 글자 단위로 같다.
    - 로그의 LLM 호출 수가 1 + 3 × 섹션 수, 검색 요청 수가 섹션 수 × 2다.
    - 세 실행의 설정값(§2.2 표)이 같다.
  - `> 관찰` 블록과 §8: `analysis/running_example_observations.py`에 있다. 근거·캡션·로그·코드와 대조해 사람이 썼다.
- **표시**: [확인] 코드·데이터로 확인 / [대조] 근거·캡션과 직접 비교 / [측정] 계산값 / [부분 확인] 존재는 확인했으나 영향 정도는 미측정 / [가설] 근거 부족·실험 없음.
- **원문 위치**: 전체 프롬프트·근거 원문은 `internal/inspect/p9p19_check_20261025_141401/<보고서>/`(`analysis/export_stages.py`)에 있다. 영상별 분리본(이 문서 이전 판)은 `backups/running_example_split_20261102/`에 보관했고 `analysis/build_running_example.py`로 다시 만들 수 있다.
- **주의**
  - 세 보고서는 각 영상의 r1 한 건이다. 생성이 샘플링(temperature 0.7, seed 없음)이라 같은 조건의 r2·r3은 outline부터 다르다(`SELF_CONSISTENCY_ANALYSIS.md`, `REPORT_TEXT_REVIEW.md`).
  - "실제 장면"은 WorldMM 캡션 기준이다. 영상을 직접 보고 확인하지는 않았다.

## 1. 한눈에

<a id="s1-1"></a>

### 1.1 파이프라인

```
[2 입력]      영상 + 질의
[3 오프라인]  WorldMM 캡션 4단위 + semantic triple + visual 임베딩 → HippoRAG 그래프 4개 (사전 인덱싱)
[4 준비]      사전 확인 → 영상 개요(10min 캡션 전부) + 영상 끝 시각 → 템플릿 교체 + C0
[5 planner]   LLM 1회 → outline (섹션 6개)
[6 섹션 × 6]  query 생성(LLM) → 검색(text: 그래프 검색 → RRF → L1 필터(LLM) + semantic / image: VLM2Vec)
              → writer(LLM) → 다음 섹션 맥락(C0)
[7 후처리]    반복 문장 제거 → 결말·시작 검사 → 인용 → References·그림 → 규칙 근거 검사 → 검증
```

- 보고서 1건의 LLM 호출 = planner 1 + 섹션마다(query 1 + L1 필터 1 + writer 1) = 19회(섹션 6개).

- **checklist**: `[]`
- **설정** (각 실행의 `config_<보고서>.yaml`. 아래 값은 세 실행이 같음을 생성 시 확인했다. 실행마다 다른 것은 포트·로그·프레임 폴더뿐이다)

### 3.3 10min 캡션 = planner가 보는 영상 개요

- 라벨은 `[시작, 시작+10분)`이다. 그러나 WorldMM은 시작 시각이 창 안인 3min 캡션을 그 창에 넣으므로 실제 내용 구간이 라벨과 다를 수 있다(두 번째 열). [확인]
- 2,048토큰에 도달한 블록은 전처리 출력 상한에서 잘린 것이다(요약이 시간순으로 진행되므로 창의 뒷부분이 빠진다).

### 3.4 HippoRAG 그래프 (단위마다 1개, `WorldMM/output/memory/videomme_long_qwen3vl-8b/report_framework_index/<영상>/episodic_memory/<단위>/`)

- 그래프 구성: 캡션 1개 = passage 노드 1개. 캡션의 OpenIE triple에서 주어·목적어가 entity 노드가 된다. 엣지는 세 종류다: fact(entity–entity, 가중치 = 횟수), passage–entity(1.0), synonym(entity 임베딩 유사도 ≥ 0.8).
- 임베딩은 Qwen3-Embedding-4B(instruction 없음, 정규화)로 만든다(`REPORT_PIPELINE.md` ④-2(b-0)).
- 엣지 수는 igraph 엣지 수 그대로다(fact 엣지는 두 방향이 각각 들어 있음). 종류는 passage 노드 포함 여부와 가중치가 정수인지로 나눴다.

| `-QuCz7kxBr8` | `100373700` | 153 / 173 | `player`(20), `man`(19), `basketball court`(9), `basketball`(7), `third man`(6) | `(Straight Shooter Strap, is, black strap)`; `(Straight Shooter Strap, is shown in, close-up)`; `(black elbow strap, is used for, elbow injury prevention)` | 226개, 차원 1536 |
| `0RxMZBLeqRI` | `100303200` | 405 / 490 | `video segment`(17), `narration`(12), `Gypsies`(11), `Roma`(9), `mounted warriors`(9) | `(Gypsy, is a term for, Roma)`; `(Gypsy, is not intended as, a slur)`; `(Roma, face lack of research, affecting societal knowledge)` | 184개, 차원 1536 |

- semantic triple에는 시간 정보가 없다. visual 임베딩은 VLM2Vec-V2로 만들었고, 50개 영상 전처리 설정은 구간당 10프레임, 최대 360×420픽셀이다(`process_one_video.sh --num-frames 10`).

<a id="s6"></a>

## 6. 섹션별 처리

<a id="s6-0"></a>

### 6.0 공통 처리 (모든 섹션)

| 단계 | 하는 일 | LLM |
|---|---|---|
| (a) query 생성 | 질의, checklist, **앞 섹션 요약(C0)**, 섹션 설명·checklist를 넣어 text query 2–3개(키워드형)와 image query 1–2개(장면 묘사)를 JSON으로 받음 | 1회 |
| (b) 검색 | text: query × 4단위 HippoRAG 그래프 검색(단위별 후보 3/3/2/1) → RRF 병합 → **L1 필터**(LLM이 episodic 8개 선택) + semantic 4개. image: VLM2Vec 텍스트→비디오 유사도 상위 3구간 → 구간 중앙 프레임 + 같은 시작 시각의 10sec 캡션 | 1회(L1 필터) |
| (c) writer | 섹션 위치, 설명·checklist, C0 요약 + 직전 섹션 끝 3조각, 근거(text `content` 전문 txt1–12, image는 캡션 문자열만 img1–3), 규칙(Grounding 1–7, Citation 1–4, 위치별, 결론, 형식) → 섹션 본문 | 1회 |
| (d) 후처리 | 반복 문장 제거, 결말·시작 서술 검사, 인용 → 전역 번호·그림, 규칙 근거 검사, 이미지-텍스트 시간 차 기록 | 0회 |
- (a)와 (c)에 들어가는 앞 섹션 요약(C0)은 직전 섹션들의 writer 출력으로 만든다. 같은 시점의 같은 요약이 두 단계에 들어간다.
- L1 필터의 후보 목록과 응답 원문은 기록되지 않는다(토큰·시간만 서버 로그에 있음).
- 근거 표의 "전역 번호"는 최종 `report.md`의 References 번호이고, 그림은 Figure 번호다. 인용 여부는 반복 제거 후 본문 기준이다.

- planner 설명: This section introduces the six main participants—Chris, Zach, Cass, James, Mitchell, and an unnamed sixth player—and establishes the setting: a sunny outdoor basketball court. It describes how they split into teams and begin testing 12 viral sports gadgets, starting with the SPORTS DRIBBLE SPECS. Readers learn the video’s goal is to test and evaluate these gadgets in a casual, competitive environment.
- checklist: List the six main participants and how they are introduced / Describe the outdoor basketball court setting and weather / Note the first gadget tested and the rules of its challenge

**(a) query 생성** — 프롬프트 438토큰, 출력 84토큰, `stop`, 3.8초

- 입력 중 앞 섹션 요약(C0):

```
This is the first section
```

- 출력(파싱 결과):
  - text 1: `six players introduced: Chris, Zach, Cass, James, Mitchell, and sixth unnamed player`
  - text 2: `first gadget tested: SPORTS DRIBBLE SPECS, rules explained for challenge`
  - image 1: `six people standing on a sunny outdoor basketball court, wearing casual sportswear, ready to play`

**(b) 검색** — text 요청 `{'video_id': '-QuCz7kxBr8', 'mode': 'L1', 'queries': 2, 'episodic_candidates': 17, 'episodic_filter': 'llm', 'counts': {'episodic': 8, 'semantic': 4}, 'elapsed_sec': 12.19}`; image 요청 `{'video_id': '-QuCz7kxBr8', 'mode': 'L1', 'queries': 1, 'counts': {'visual_clips': 3, 'frames': 3}, 'elapsed_sec': 1.28}`

- text query 2개 × 4단위 그래프 검색 → RRF → L1 필터(프롬프트 8661토큰, 출력 66토큰, 4.4초) → episodic 8개 + semantic 4개. image query 1개 → 프레임 3장.

# Depiction of Roma as Historically Misclassified and Systematically Stigmatized

At 00:00:30, the video presents a man in a yellow lab coat carefully transferring liquid with a pipette, symbolizing scientific precision or experimentation. This image is immediately followed by a black-and-white depiction of a man in a lab coat marked with a large red “X,” suggesting exclusion from scientific or societal norms [citation:txt3]. The juxtaposition of these two figures—scientifically engaged yet rejected—visually critiques how Roma have been subjected to exclusionary frameworks even within academic and institutional domains. The scene then transitions to cultural imagery: a man in a red sweater gesturing before a group in traditional clothing, some dancing, followed by black-and-white photos of a band playing traditional instruments and a family with children holding instruments seated before a wagon, evoking heritage and communal life [citation:txt3]. These images culminate in the word “UNWANTED” superimposed over historical scenes, accompanied by a voiceover explaining how the vast majority of Roma have been historically stigmatized and labeled as unwanted nuisances [citation:txt1]. This visual and auditory combination underscores the systemic erasure and dehumanization embedded in historical narratives.

The video then transitions to a Minecraft gameplay scene where a player mines, symbolizing labor or resource extraction [citation:txt2]. This is followed by a cut to a menacing, horned humanoid character declaring “Your money or your life,” evoking themes of coercion or economic exploitation [citation:txt2]. The tone shifts to a dark fantasy setting with robed figures in combat, followed by a surreal image of a black, hooded figure with glowing dollar signs, suggesting corruption or the commodification of power [citation:txt2]. These fantasy scenes serve as allegory for how Roma are often reduced to archetypes of “danger” or “criminality,” despite their rich cultural contributions. The video contrasts this with vibrant dance performances—on stage and in public squares—representing joy, freedom, or resistance [citation:txt2]. The segment concludes with a somber black-and-white photograph of displaced people sitting on the ground, underscoring suffering and loss [citation:txt2]. Throughout, the voiceover traces the tragic history behind stereotypes of thieves and black magic casters, framing them as products of societal fear and misunderstanding [citation:txt2]. This sequence effectively links Roma identity to geopolitical misreading and societal fear, using satirical fantasy and cultural imagery to critique how they are reduced to stereotypes.

The video’s depiction of scientific exclusion is further reinforced by the lab-coated figure and the red “X”-marked scientist, symbolizing how Roma have been systematically excluded from scholarly and institutional frameworks [citation:txt3]. The “UNWANTED” text superimposed over historical scenes directly references the video’s central argument: that Roma have been historically misclassified and stigmatized, not as a result of inherent traits, but as a product of societal fear and geopolitical misreading [citation:txt1]. The transition from Minecraft mining to fantasy combat and back to dance and displacement illustrates the video’s thematic arc: from labor and exploitation to cultural resistance and enduring suffering [citation:txt2]. The use of fantasy and game-based visuals, juxtaposed with historical and cultural imagery, serves to highlight the absurdity and harm of reducing Roma identity to simplistic, often violent, stereotypes [citation:txt5]. This section thus critiques how Roma are not only misclassified but also rendered invisible, feared, and commodified within historical and contemporary narratives.

# Historical Narrative of Roma Origins and Early Misidentification

At 00:01:00, the video introduces the enigma of Roma origins, opening with a map animation tracing migration from the Middle East and South Asia into Europe. This visual anchors the Roma’s presence in the Balkans since the 13th century, while a 3D figure holding a red question mark symbolizes the enduring mystery surrounding their origins [citation:txt1]. The narrative then transitions to a stylized 13th-century map of Europe and the Balkans, featuring a dancing woman in traditional attire — visually anchoring Roma cultural presence in the region [citation:txt3]. This map is followed by a depiction of a faceless crowd and a red arrow pointing toward the Balkans, indicating movement or migration [citation:txt3].

At 00:01:10, the video presents a “VS” graphic, introducing a symbolic conflict between the Seljuk Turks — represented by an illustrated figure wearing a red fez — and the Byzantine Empire, symbolized by a crowned figure [citation:txt3][citation:txt11]. The narration explicitly frames this as a geopolitical tension of the era, setting the stage for how Roma would later be misidentified [citation:txt3]. The scene transitions to a map highlighting the Balkans again, overlaid by a man in a red shirt, white shorts, and fez, seemingly walking along the arrow’s path — visually suggesting migration [citation:txt2]. This is followed by a historical battle scene with mounted soldiers, blue banners, and fallen warriors, reinforcing the context of warfare between Christian and Muslim forces [citation:txt2].

The narration explains that the first Gypsy arrivals were mistaken for Seljuk Turks by the Byzantines, due to the ongoing conflicts between Christian Europe and Muslim Turks [citation:txt1][citation:txt2]. The video thus positions Roma not as a distinct ethnic group but as a product of historical misreading and geopolitical conflict — their arrival coinciding with the collapse of empires and the rise of new identities [citation:txt5]. The visual narrative reinforces how Roma were not “invented” but rather misclassified, their identity embedded in the historical and political landscape of the time [citation:txt5]. The imagery of the battle, combined with the “VS” graphic, underscores how Roma were labeled by empires caught in the crossfire of imperial rivalry [citation:txt3].

The video further frames this misidentification as part of a broader pattern of historical erasure, where Roma were categorized as “foreign” and “dangerous” through religious and cultural binaries — as seen in the transition to a medieval battle painting with the text “SARACEN = HEATHENS” [citation:txt5]. This visual and narrative framing positions Roma as a product of historical misreading, shaped by the victors’ geopolitical narratives [citation:txt5]. The use of symbolic figures, maps, and battle imagery serves to show how Roma were labeled by empires — not as an ethnic group, but as a consequence of historical conflict and misreading [citation:txt5]. The video thus concludes this section by reinforcing that Roma were not “invented” but misclassified — their identity forged in the crucible of empire and war [citation:txt5].

# Conclusion

The video portrays the Roma as a people marked by historical marginalization, yet enduring through systemic persecution with remarkable cultural resilience. From its opening disclaimer affirming the non-slandrous use of “Gypsy,” the video frames Roma identity as both deeply rooted in Balkan history — evidenced by sepia-toned photographs of families in traditional attire and modern parades featuring Roma flags alongside EU and Ukrainian banners — and persistently misunderstood, as shown by recurring visual motifs of exclusion, such as the “X”-marked scientist and the “UNWANTED” overlay on historical scenes [1][3]. The narrative traces their origins from South Asia through the Ghaznavid Empire and into Byzantine territories, where they were misidentified as Seljuk Turks, embedding their identity within geopolitical conflict [20]. This historical misclassification and subsequent institutionalization under Nazi and communist regimes — though the latter is only referenced via a title card — are depicted as tools of erasure, with archival visuals of Gestapo mugshots and bureaucratic “Zigeuner” labels reinforcing state-sanctioned persecution [3][3]. Despite this, the video highlights moments of quiet resistance: a Roma woman asserting “I am also a Roma” at a rally, a dancing boy in front of a satellite-dish-covered building, and an animated character symbolizing cultural endurance — all underscoring resilience amid systemic oppression [21]. The video concludes not with a resolution but with a global perspective, transitioning to a stylized globe rotating against a backdrop of international flags, before fading to black — a visual that frames Roma experiences as part of a broader, interconnected global narrative (Figure 6) (Figure 7). Credits appear at 00:30:08, marking the formal end of the video’s content [22]. This final sequence confirms the video’s focus on Roma identity, historical marginalization, systemic persecution, and cultural resilience — all synthesized through layered visuals, historical context, and symbolic imagery.

The video opens with a segment from CBC News’ “The National,” hosted by Ian Henneman, delivering a public health report on the resurgence of measles in Canadian communities [citation:txt4]. Within the first minute, the video transitions to footage of a Canadian swimmer, Joshua Liendo, competing in a butterfly stroke race, followed by interview segments where he reflects on his journey as a trailblazer for Black swimmers [citation:txt4]. This athletic segment serves as a contrast to the public health narrative, briefly shifting focus before returning to the measles outbreak. The swimmer’s story is framed as a commentary on rising prominence and potential Olympic impact, but it is quickly superseded by the return to the health report.

At 00:01:30, the video juxtaposes everyday family life — a man swinging a child at a Toronto playground — with the ongoing public health concern, as the same news ticker continues to appear [citation:txt5]. The scene then shifts to a bearded parent speaking outdoors near bare trees, followed by shots of crowded streets and a stadium crowd, all under the persistent warning of measles spread [citation:txt5]. This visual contrast highlights the tension between normalcy and emerging public health threats.

The video introduces Dr. Earl Rubin from Montreal Children’s Hospital, who addresses the camera, stating that the measles situation reflects only the tip of the iceberg and questions the origin of the outbreak — underscoring the scale and mystery of the spread [citation:txt5]. Dr. Rubin’s remarks are followed by a scene of a medical professional reviewing paperwork near a patient cart, reinforcing the clinical context of the outbreak [citation:txt3].

At 00:02:00, Dr. Anna Banerji, a pediatric infectious diseases specialist in Parry Sound, Ontario, is introduced. She explains how the measles virus can linger in the air in hospital or waiting room environments, potentially exposing new individuals [citation:txt2]. The segment transitions to footage of a healthcare worker administering the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine, illustrating prevention efforts [citation:txt2].

On-screen text during this segment notes that Canada officially eliminated measles in 1998, but vaccination rates have since declined [citation:txt2]. This is reinforced by another text overlay later in the segment, which states that current vaccination levels stand at 79% [citation:txt1].

Dr. Christopher Labos, an epidemiologist in Montreal, is also featured, speaking to the camera and gesturing as he explains that if community spread of measles begins, more cases will follow [citation:txt6]. The video’s opening segments thus establish a public health report framing, centered on the resurgence of measles, the role of medical experts, and the risks posed by declining vaccination rates and the virus’s environmental persistence.

# Unfolding Public Health Crisis: Measles Outbreak, Hospital Tragedy, and Emergency Response Failures

At 00:03:00, the video shifts focus to a measles outbreak in the United States, with 41 confirmed cases across 16 states, centered on Manatee Bay Elementary near Fort Lauderdale, Florida [citation:txt5]. The outbreak poses heightened risk to unvaccinated and immunocompromised children under one year of age [citation:txt5]. Parent Demi Cavanaugh is shown expressing concern for her unvaccinated son, who cannot receive his second vaccine until age four and is at high risk for complications, while her vaccinated daughter remains protected [citation:txt5]. Visuals include a child receiving a vaccine under protective measures, aerial shots of the school, and community scenes highlighting parental anxiety [citation:txt5]. Public health officials warn of potential spread into Canadian communities, prompting CBC News to issue urgent vaccination advisories [citation:txt5]. Anchors and medical experts stress the importance of early vaccination (as early as nine months) and maternal antibodies for infant protection, urging consultation with healthcare providers [citation:txt7].

Simultaneously, the video documents a third patient death in a Montreal hospital waiting room, which is currently under coroner’s review [citation:txt4]. This follows a prior fatality caused by a 45-minute ambulance delay due to insufficient resources [citation:txt4]. Authorities are investigating systemic resource shortages, with medical professionals warning that without increased emergency vehicle deployment, similar tragedies are inevitable [citation:txt4]. Footage shows hospital corridors, triage areas, and paramedics preparing ambulances, underscoring strained emergency response [citation:txt4]. A man in a white shirt with a red collar is shown warning during an interview that if patient transportation isn’t prioritized by adding vehicles, similar tragic events are certain to recur [citation:txt8][citation:txt11]. The scene cuts to a low-angle shot of a hospital hallway, where a gurney is visible and medical staff in scrubs walk in the background, with a news banner at the bottom reading, “Coroner investigating 3rd death in Quebec hospital waiting room” [citation:img1][citation:txt8].

The video juxtaposes these domestic crises with international affairs. At 00:04:50, a news studio segment shows a male anchor reporting on the Quebec case, while a screen behind him displays footage of a woman speaking at a podium with the seal of the President of the United States [citation:img3]. On-screen text identifies the news story as “Coroner investigating 3rd death in Quebec hospital waiting room” and later, “U.S. vice-president calls for ‘immediate ceasefire’ in Gaza” [citation:img3]. This contrast highlights the simultaneous unfolding of a public health emergency and political developments, reinforcing the video’s narrative of intersecting national and global crises.

Visuals of hospital corridors and paramedics preparing ambulances are repeatedly shown, reinforcing the strain on emergency services [citation:txt4][citation:txt7]. These scenes appear alongside on-screen alerts and news tickers that emphasize the urgency of the measles outbreak and the hospital tragedy [citation:txt4][citation:txt7]. The footage underscores the systemic failures in emergency response and the public health risks posed by declining vaccination rates and resource shortages [citation:txt4][citation:txt1].

The video’s coverage of the measles outbreak and hospital deaths is framed within a broader context of public health alarm. Dr. Christopher Labos, previously mentioned in the prior section, is referenced again in the context of the measles resurgence, warning that once community transmission begins, outbreaks escalate, particularly endangering young children and immunocompromised individuals [citation:txt1]. This reinforces the video’s central theme: the fragility of public health systems in the face of preventable diseases and systemic under-resourcing.

The segment concludes with continued coverage of the Quebec hospital death and the U.S. measles outbreak, maintaining the video’s focus on urgent, unfolding crises. The juxtaposition of domestic health emergencies with international political developments underscores the interconnected nature of these issues, as highlighted in the video’s earlier segments [citation:txt4][citation:txt7]. The visuals and on-screen text consistently reinforce the gravity of the situation, emphasizing the need for immediate public health action and systemic reform.

# Shift to Personal Tragedy and Institutional Failure, Followed by Athletic Triumph

At 00:20:00, the video transitions into a segment focused on a misidentification tragedy at Montfort Hospital, which occurred on February 23, 2024. The incident involved a deceased patient who was mourned by grieving family members as their son — only to later be verified as a stranger. The hospital issued an official statement, addressed to “Daniel,” referencing the Office of the Chief Coroner of Ontario and the Ottawa Paramedic Service, and confirmed that affected families have been informed. A formal review is underway to address systemic failures [citation:txt1][citation:txt2]. CBC News coverage of the event includes on-screen text and visuals of hospital exteriors, interviews with Jennifer Zelmer of Healthcare Excellence Canada, and emotional family members [citation:txt1].

Heather Insley, identified as a mother from Picton, Ontario, is shown in a CBC News interview recounting how her family mourned the death of their son before realizing he was a stranger [citation:txt3][citation:txt4]. She is seated in a warmly lit home setting with a stained-glass lamp behind her, holding a smartphone and speaking candidly to an interviewer, her expression heavy with sorrow [citation:txt3][citation:txt4]. The video juxtaposes this intimate moment with hospital scenes showing a critically ill patient connected to life-support equipment and a healthcare worker in protective gear attending to them [citation:txt3][citation:img1]. On-screen text underscores the emotional gravity of the story: “Family mourns son’s death before realizing it was a stranger” [citation:txt10][citation:img1].

The emotional aftermath is further illustrated by a grieving woman in a red sweater and glasses, speaking to an interviewer in a living room, her sorrow evident as she reflects on the loss of her son — only to later discover he was a stranger [citation:txt6][citation:txt7]. The video intercuts this with a somber man in a red plaid hoodie and black cap, seen washing his hands and meticulously wiping down a stove in a kitchen, where a Pepsi bottle and cigarette box sit untouched; his somber demeanor underscores the weight of the revelation [citation:txt6]. Footage of Sean Cox, identified as the son, is shown speaking directly to the camera, before returning to the woman on the couch, still absorbed in her phone, as the on-screen text and CBC News logo reinforce the tragic misunderstanding [citation:txt6].

The narrative then shifts abruptly to a competitive swimming event, showcasing medalists and training sequences, before cutting to a title card for “The National” [citation:txt2]. A scene of a building engulfed in flames, blanketed in snow, introduces a new segment, establishing the aftermath of a destructive event [citation:txt2]. The video then transitions to a CBC News anchor introducing the growing trend of self-taping for film and TV auditions, featuring interviews with industry figures like Joel Montgrand and Deirdre Bowen [citation:txt2][citation:txt6].

However, the video’s primary focus in this section is the institutional failure at Montfort Hospital and its human cost. The CBC News report, illustrated with on-screen text and visuals including hospital exteriors and interviews with Jennifer Zelmer and a grieving family, underscores the emotional toll and institutional response to the error [citation:txt1]. The hospital’s official statement and formal review are clearly documented, confirming the systemic nature of the failure [citation:txt5].

The segment concludes with a transition to athletic triumph: Canadian swimmer Joshua Liendo, representing the Florida Gators, wins gold in the Men’s 100m Butterfly at the Commonwealth Games [citation:txt2][citation:txt8]. The video showcases his training, competition highlights, and medal celebration, including teammates waving the Canadian flag [citation:txt2][citation:txt8]. A CBC News anchor frames his story as historic, concluding with on-screen text declaring him “swims into the history books” [citation:txt2]. Liendo is shown seated poolside in a white Gators shirt and gold chain, discussing his breakthrough season and crediting the University of Florida’s training environment [citation:txt2][citation:txt9]. The video closes with Liendo’s legacy firmly anchored in both Canadian and American swimming history, as the CBC anchor reinforces his place among Olympic greats [citation:txt2][citation:txt10].

The video’s structure juxtaposes the personal tragedy of misidentification with the public celebration of athletic achievement, highlighting the contrast between institutional failure and human resilience. The emotional weight of the hospital error is balanced by Liendo’s triumph, symbolizing not only athletic excellence but also the emotional resilience required to navigate life’s unpredictable turns [citation:txt2]. The narrative arc moves from loss to performance, from chaos to clarity, and ultimately, from tragedy to triumph [citation:txt2].

# Community Disaster and Recovery

At 00:36:00, a devastating fire destroyed the only school on Eabametoong First Nation, located in Northwestern Ontario, leaving behind charred ruins blanketed in snow [citation:txt1][citation:txt2]. The blaze overwhelmed local firefighting efforts due to inadequate water infrastructure, forcing children to relocate for education and deepening grief among residents [citation:txt1][citation:txt2]. Four teenagers have been charged in connection with the arson [citation:txt1]. Community members, including teacher Mary Okeese and student Owen Slipperjack, shared emotional testimonies contrasting joyful school memories with the current devastation [citation:txt1][citation:txt2]. Chief Solomon Atlookan emphasized systemic vulnerabilities in emergency response for remote Indigenous communities [citation:txt1][citation:txt2]. Aerial and ground footage underscored the isolation of the community, 360 km from Winnipeg, near Thunder Bay [citation:txt1][citation:txt2]. The Canadian and First Nations flags fly at half-mast as the community mourns and begins the long road to recovery [citation:txt1][citation:txt2].

In response to the crisis, the federal government pledged over $13 million to construct five modular classrooms as temporary solutions, aiming to restore educational continuity for affected children [citation:txt1][citation:txt2][citation:txt5][citation:txt6]. This pledge was confirmed after the Federal Minister of Indigenous Services met with the chief in Thunder Bay [citation:txt5][citation:txt6]. The government’s commitment was reiterated in a CBC News segment, where officials vowed to stand with the community in constructing a new permanent school [citation:txt3][citation:txt4]. The video shows the aftermath of the fire, with footage of the collapsed metal roof under a cloudy sky, alongside Canadian and First Nation flags [citation:txt3][citation:txt4][citation:txt5][citation:txt6]. A memorial ceremony was held in a gymnasium, followed by footage of the “Rev. Eleazar Winter Memorial School” sign and a large nighttime fire, confirming the school’s destruction [citation:txt1][citation:txt4].

By June 2023, Pikangikum First Nation unveiled its newly built school — a modern facility with vehicles parked outside — symbolizing a decade-long wait for replacement after the original school was lost to fire [citation:txt3][citation:txt8]. The narration underscores the urgency of the rebuild, highlighting the community’s prolonged struggle for educational infrastructure [citation:txt3][citation:txt8]. In September 2023, Wapekeka First Nation celebrated the grand opening of its new school — a colorful, modern building adorned with festive decorations, balloons, and banners [citation:txt3][citation:txt7]. The event marked the end of an eight-year wait following the fire, showcasing community resilience and the government’s eventual fulfillment of long-delayed promises [citation:txt3][citation:txt7]. # Conclusion

The video presents a layered narrative that intertwines public health crises, institutional failures, and athletic triumph, ultimately concluding with themes of community recovery and athletic legacy. Public health concerns are prominently featured, including a measles outbreak in the United States with 41 confirmed cases and a third patient death in a Montreal hospital, underscoring systemic vulnerabilities in emergency response and disease containment [citation:txt1][citation:txt2]. These crises are juxtaposed with institutional failures, such as the misidentification tragedy at Montfort Hospital, where a grieving family mourned the loss of a son only to later discover he was a stranger — a case that highlights profound systemic breakdowns in healthcare [citation:txt3]. The video also documents the devastating fire that destroyed the only school on Eabametoong First Nation, leaving behind charred ruins and triggering a community-wide crisis, with inadequate infrastructure and delayed government support compounding the trauma [citation:txt4][citation:txt5][citation:txt6]. Yet, the narrative pivots toward recovery, showing the eventual construction of new schools in Pikangikum and Wapekeka First Nations, symbolizing resilience and the fulfillment of long-delayed promises [citation:txt7][citation:txt8].

In parallel, the video celebrates athletic triumph through the story of Joshua Liendo, Canada’s first Black swimmer to win international gold in the 100-meter butterfly at the Doha World Championships. His journey — from Trinidad to Toronto, from childhood in a Caribbean community to global podiums — is framed as both personal achievement and a broader cultural milestone [citation:txt1]. Liendo’s reflections on role models, systemic underrepresentation, and the sacrifices of his family underscore his legacy not only as an athlete but as a symbol of progress and representation in elite swimming [citation:txt1]. His victory, captured in dynamic race footage and celebrated by a roaring Canadian crowd, marks a historic moment that contrasts sharply with the tragedies and institutional failures depicted earlier [citation:txt1]. The video concludes by returning to the themes of recovery and legacy: the rebuilding of schools and the enduring hope of First Nation communities, alongside Liendo’s enduring presence as a trailblazer, affirming that resilience and triumph can emerge even in the face of profound loss [citation:txt7][citation:txt8].

# Conclusion

The video presents a layered narrative that intertwines public health crises, institutional failures, and athletic triumph, ultimately concluding with themes of community recovery and athletic legacy. Public health concerns are prominently featured, including a measles outbreak in the United States with 41 confirmed cases and a third patient death in a Montreal hospital, underscoring systemic vulnerabilities in emergency response and disease containment [32][33]. These crises are juxtaposed with institutional failures, such as the misidentification tragedy at Montfort Hospital, where a grieving family mourned the loss of a son only to later discover he was a stranger — a case that highlights profound systemic breakdowns in healthcare [37]. The video also documents the devastating fire that destroyed the only school on Eabametoong First Nation, leaving behind charred ruins and triggering a community-wide crisis, with inadequate infrastructure and delayed government support compounding the trauma [40][38][41]. Yet, the narrative pivots toward recovery, showing the eventual construction of new schools in Pikangikum and Wapekeka First Nations, symbolizing resilience and the fulfillment of long-delayed promises [35][42].

In parallel, the video celebrates athletic triumph through the story of Joshua Liendo, Canada’s first Black swimmer to win international gold in the 100-meter butterfly at the Doha World Championships. His journey — from Trinidad to Toronto, from childhood in a Caribbean community to global podiums — is framed as both personal achievement and a broader cultural milestone [32]. Liendo’s reflections on role models, systemic underrepresentation, and the sacrifices of his family underscore his legacy not only as an athlete but as a symbol of progress and representation in elite swimming [32]. His victory, captured in dynamic race footage and celebrated by a roaring Canadian crowd, marks a historic moment that contrasts sharply with the tragedies and institutional failures depicted earlier [32]. The video concludes by returning to the themes of recovery and legacy: the rebuilding of schools and the enduring hope of First Nation communities, alongside Liendo’s enduring presence as a trailblazer, affirming that resilience and triumph can emerge even in the face of profound loss [35][42].
```

## 9. 재생성 방법과 발표 활용

```bash
cd report_framework
python -B analysis/build_running_example_combined.py          # 이 문서 (internal/running_example/RUNNING_EXAMPLE.md)
# (선택) 영상별 분리본: build_running_example.py --video=<vid> 후 running_example_observations.py
python -B analysis/export_stages.py                         # internal/inspect/: 프롬프트·근거 원문 전체
# §10의 검색 내부 과정 (CPU 8코어, 약 10분): 결과 results/retrieval_repro_-QuCz7kxBr8_r1.json
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES= python -B analysis/reproduce_retrieval_cpu.py --video=-QuCz7kxBr8 --work-dir <임시 폴더>
```

|---|---|

| 한 섹션의 query → 근거 15개(인용 여부·전역 번호) → writer 원문 → 최종 본문 | §6.1.1 (`-QuCz7kxBr8` 섹션 1), §6.3.3 (`54k2g9ddy4M` 섹션 3) |

## 10. 발표용 심층 예시: `-QuCz7kxBr8` (농구 가젯 시험) 보고서 r1의 모든 중간 산출물

<a id="s10-0"></a>

### 10.0 이 절의 범위와 읽는 법

- **대상**: §6.1의 보고서와 같은 건(`outputs/p9p19_check_20261025_141401/-QuCz7kxBr8__c0_written__r1`). §2–§7이 세 영상을 비교했다면, 이 절은 한 영상에 대해 **사전 구축 메모리의 실제 내용, 모듈이 실제로 받은 프레임, 모듈별 입력·출력 원문**을 모두 펼친다.
- **만든 방법**: `analysis/build_running_example_deep.py`가 아래 원본에서 직접 생성했다(LLM 재호출 없음, CPU).
  - WorldMM 전처리 결과: `WorldMM/output/memory/videomme_long_qwen3vl-8b/` 아래 caption·transcript·metadata, 전처리 로그 `logs/-QuCz7kxBr8.log`
  - WorldMM 코드를 수정 없이 불러와 다시 계산: 10초 구간 분할·캡션 입력 프레임(`preprocess/episodic_memory/generate_fine_caption.py`), VLM2Vec 프레임 범위·리사이즈(`VLM2Vec/.../qwen_vl_utils.py`), 캡션 계층 묶음(`gen_multiscale._summarize_level`과 같은 규칙)

### 10.2 10sec 캡션 생성: 캡션 모델이 실제로 받은 프레임과 프롬프트

- 모델: Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (`--model qwen3vl-8b`), 최대 출력 2,048토큰(`qwen3vl.py` 기본값). [확인]
- 프레임: 구간 안의 **매 정수 초마다 1장**(`compute_sample_seconds`), 프레임 번호 = round(초 × fps). 10초 구간이면 10장. 원본 1280×720 프레임을 PIL 이미지로 그대로 넘긴다(모델 안의 리사이즈는 `qwen_vl_utils`·processor 기본값이며 여기서는 측정하지 않음). [확인]
- 메시지: system(아래 프롬프트) + user[구간 시각, 겹치는 자막 줄, 그리고 프레임마다 `Frame timestamp: …` 문자열 + 이미지]. [확인]

<details><summary>캡션 system 프롬프트 원문 (`generate_fine_caption.py` SYSTEM_PROMPT)</summary>

```
You are an expert video captioner.

You will receive a short video segment represented by ordered frames and optional transcript lines with timestamps.
Write a caption describing both the visual content and the audible content of the segment.

Guidelines:
- Describe visible actions, people, objects, and environment.
- Include relevant speech, sounds, or audio events.
- Keep the caption factual and neutral.
- Do not mention frames, timestamps, or that the input came from frames.
- Avoid speculation about emotions or intentions unless clearly visible or stated in speech.

Output only the final caption text.
```

</details>

### 10.3 episodic memory ①: 캡션 4단위 계층의 실제 내용

- 만드는 방법(`worldmm.memory.episodic.gen_multiscale`, perspective `general`) [확인]
  - 30sec ← 10sec, 3min ← 30sec, 10min ← 3min. 바로 아래 단위의 캡션을 시작 시각 순으로 창(30/180/600초)에 묶는다. 첫 창은 첫 캡션 시각에서, 다음 창은 `(시작 // 창) × 창`에서 시작한다.
  - 묶인 캡션 text를 줄바꿈으로 이어 `All descriptions: …` 한 덩어리로 LLM에 준다(**시각 표기 없음**). system 프롬프트는 단계별 L1/L2/L3이며, 출력 형식 문장의 단어 제한만 다르다(없음 / 300단어 / 1,500단어).
  - 결과의 start/end는 창의 시작·끝(창 크기 그대로)이다. 그래서 마지막 창의 끝은 영상 끝보다 뒤일 수 있다.
- 다시 묶어 본 결과: 10sec 226 → 30sec 76 → 3min 13 → 10min 4. 창 개수·시작·끝이 파일과 모두 같다. [확인]

| 단위 | 항목 수 | 단어 수 평균 / 최소 / 최대 | 한 항목이 덮는 아래 단위 개수 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10sec | 226 | 85 / 43 / 137 | — |
| 30sec | 76 | 168 / 63 / 272 | 1개×1, 3개×75 |
| 3min | 13 | 310 / 137 / 383 | 4개×1, 6개×12 |
| 10min | 4 | 816 / 624 / 1265 | 3개×3, 4개×1 |

#### 10.3.1 00:00:00–00:03:00 전체 계층 (원문 그대로)

Six men—Chris, Zach, Cass, James, Mitchell, and a sixth unnamed player—gather on a sunny outdoor basketball court to test 12 viral sports gadgets, splitting into two teams of three. Dressed in athletic wear, they introduce the challenge while holding basketballs near a hoop and trees. One man in a white hoodie addresses the camera, setting the tone with playful banter and audio cues like “Hands up, hands up” and “Mump is blinding me.” The scene transitions to a countdown and gear review, beginning with a close-up of black nylon straps, signaling the start of hands-on testing.

The group begins evaluating gadgets, starting with “SPORTS DRIBBLE SPECS.” One player dons the goggles and prepares for a dribbling time trial, where participants must dribble through three cones and touch a pole to stop the clock. Rules are clarified near a pool under bright sunlight, with the man in the hoodie confirming the forfeit rule for the slowest time. The drill proceeds with players like Chris and Zach showcasing speed and control, with timers capturing times like 10:85 and 9:51 seconds. Commentary highlights frustrations (“handles were definitely off”) and praise (“He’s making great time”), emphasizing the competitive yet casual atmosphere.

Later, the group discusses the gadget’s usefulness, with the man in the white hoodie expressing discomfort with traditional basketballs forcing him to look down. A score graphic flashes from 5 to 6, then 4, as teammates react with thumbs-up approval. The segment ends with the introduction of the SKLZ Dribble Stick—a black training tool with adjustable yellow arms—where the blue-jerseyed player prepares to demonstrate its use. Rules are reviewed: players dribble while avoiding the stick; the first to touch it runs five laps. The group is ready to begin, setting up for the next round of testing.
```

**Six men—Chris, Zach, Cass, James, Mitchell, and an unnamed sixth player—gather on a sunny outdoor basketball court to test 12 viral sports gadgets, splitting into two teams of three. The group begins evaluating gadgets, starting with “SPORTS DRIBBLE SPECS.” One player dons the goggles and prepares for a dribbling time trial, where participants must dribble through three cones and touch a pole to stop the clock. Rules are clarified near a pool under bright sunlight, with the man in the hoodie confirming the forfeit rule for the slowest time. The drill proceeds with players like Chris and Zach showcasing speed and control, with timers capturing times like 10:85 and 9:51 seconds. Commentary highlights frustrations (“handles were definitely off”) and praise (“He’s making great time”), emphasizing the competitive yet casual atmosphere.

Later, the group discusses the gadget’s usefulness, with the man in the white hoodie expressing discomfort with traditional basketballs forcing him to look down. A score graphic flashes from 5 to 6, then 4, as teammates react with thumbs-up approval. The segment ends with the introduction of the SKLZ Dribble Stick—a black training tool with adjustable yellow arms—where the blue-jerseyed player prepares to demonstrate its use. Rules are reviewed: players dribble while avoiding the stick; the first to touch it runs five laps. The group is ready to begin, setting up for the next round of testing.

**Three men gather on an outdoor basketball court, negotiating positions before settling into a shooting challenge. One man in a black hoodie and white cap adjusts a basketball on a training device while the others—wearing red and blue jerseys—observe, holding balls. A fourth person films the scene under clear skies, with trees and a fence in the background. The group transitions to a hoop with a vertical obstacle, where they take turns shooting under a 30-second countdown. Encouragement and light-hearted banter—such as “you might be safe just making it past that first one”—add to the casual yet competitive tone. The man in the black hoodie successfully makes his shot, smiling as he walks back, while the man in red watches amusedly. Their conversation hints at past forfeits and humorous self-deprecation.**

The group then evaluates the dribble stick, with the man in the blue jersey rating it an 8/10, followed by the man in the black shirt agreeing, and the man in the black hoodie giving it a 7—joking that anything helping him fail is “pretty good.” The conversation remains lighthearted and collaborative.

**Later, a man in a white hoodie demonstrates the “Straight Shooter Strap,” explaining how it stabilizes the elbow during shooting. He adjusts the strap on his arm while a third observer watches. A shooter in a white shirt and patterned shorts begins a shooting sequence, initially making one shot (0/1), then missing several, with the scoreboard climbing to 0/3. **A man in a white hoodie and patterned shorts shoots basketballs on a sunny court, with a score counter updating after each shot — from 0/0 to 3/5 — while a humorous voiceover references product ownership and investment. He praises the product as “great,” with a “#NOT SPONSORED” graphic. The scene cuts to another player resetting the score.**

A second player makes a shot (1/2), but audio commentary criticizes the product’s performance, noting it “fell off” and “snaps” when extended. A shooting contest unfolds: a player in a red and white jersey (No. 2) makes a successful shot (2/5), celebrated with surprise and joy. Later, the tie-dye jersey player loses, prompting the white-shirted man to propose testing his jump shot without the strap to isolate the issue — a playful, lighthearted challenge.

His jump shot misses, sparking frustration and speculation about the strap. A teammate confirms the issue, and a forfeit of 30 jumping jacks is suggested. The man begins doing jumping jacks, arms raised, while two others watch and tease — one jokes about “bouncing titties,” another compares chest sizes. He deflects with humor, “Bro, I’m wearing a big shirt.” His movements become off-rhythm, drawing amused observation.

**Three men discuss and humorously rate the product: the white-hoodie man (ZHYPE) calls it suitable for kids but suggests a better gadget for beginners, scoring it “1.” They escalate to exaggerated scoring — “1,” “2,” then “-3k” — ending with a playful “what’s the next invention?”**

**A shooting challenge with the Flick Glove begins: one man in a black hoodie explains rules — three shots with the glove, then without — with the fewest baskets requiring 100 sit-ups. The red-hoodie man misunderstands the glove’s orientation, prompting a demonstration. The glove’s design (finger loops, screen) and color options (white, black, orange) are shown.**

The player in the red hoodie makes a shot, humorously noting the ball nearly slipped off his pinky finger. He pauses, gestures while holding a wristband, removes it, and reflects on his performance. He critiques his flick motion, acknowledging lack of straightness, before preparing for another attempt, observed by two onlookers in black and blue attire.

**Separately, the man in the black hoodie performs sit-ups on a concrete court, with on-screen text “CASH LOST,” explained by voiceover as punishment for fewest flick shots. <a id="s10-4"></a>

### 10.4 episodic memory ②: OpenIE triple과 HippoRAG 그래프

- **10sec OpenIE**(WorldMM 전처리, `build_memory.py --step episodic`): 10sec 캡션마다 LLM 2회 — NER(개체 목록) → NER을 조건으로 triple 추출. 각 호출은 최대 3회 재시도(`dynamic_retry_decorator`), 끝내 실패하면 빈 목록을 저장한다(`openie.py`). [확인]
- **다른 단위(30sec·3min·10min)**: 보고서 프레임워크의 사전 인덱싱(`prebuild_episodic_index.py`)이 같은 프롬프트로 OpenIE를 돌렸다. 10sec은 위 전처리 결과를 그대로 옮겨 썼다(seeding). [확인]

<details><summary>NER 프롬프트 (system + one-shot 예시 + 캡션)</summary>

```
[
 {
  "role": "system",
  "content": "Your task is to extract named entities from the given paragraph. \nRespond with a JSON list of entities.\n"
 },
 {
  "role": "user",
  "content": "Radio City\nRadio City is India's first private FM radio station and was started on 3 July 2001.\nIt plays Hindi, English and regional songs.\nRadio City recently forayed into New Media in May 2008 with the launch of a music portal - PlanetRadiocity.com that offers music related news, videos, songs, and other music-related features."
 },
 {
  "role": "assistant",
  "content": "{\"named_entities\":\n    [\"Radio City\", \"India\", \"3 July 2001\", \"Hindi\", \"English\", \"May 2008\", \"PlanetRadiocity.com\"]\n}\n"
 },
 {
  "role": "user",
  "content": "${passage}"
 }
]
```

</details>

<details><summary>triple 추출 프롬프트 (system + one-shot 예시 + 캡션·NER 결과)</summary>

````
[
 {
  "role": "system",
  "content": "Your task is to construct an RDF (Resource Description Framework) graph from the given passages and named entity lists. \nRespond with a JSON list of triples, with each triple representing a relationship in the RDF graph. \n\nPay attention to the following requirements:\n- Each triple should contain at least one, but preferably two, of the named entities in the list for each passage.\n- When resolving pronouns, if the pronoun refers to the first-person (e.g., I, me, my), keep it as \"I\" instead of replacing with terms like \"speaker\" or \"narrator\". For other pronouns, clearly resolve them to their specific names to maintain clarity.\n\n"
 },
 {
  "role": "user",
  "content": "Convert the paragraph into a JSON dict, it has a named entity list and a triple list.\nParagraph:\n```\nRadio City\nRadio City is India's first private FM radio station and was started on 3 July 2001.\nIt plays Hindi, English and regional songs.\nRadio City recently forayed into New Media in May 2008 with the launch of a music portal - PlanetRadiocity.com that offers music related news, videos, songs, and other music-related features.\n```\n\n{\"named_entities\":\n    [\"Radio City\", \"India\", \"3 July 2001\", \"Hindi\", \"English\", \"May 2008\", \"PlanetRadiocity.com\"]\n}\n\n"
 },
 {
  "role": "assistant",
  "content": "{\"triples\": [\n            [\"Radio City\", \"located in\", \"India\"],\n            [\"Radio City\", \"is\", \"private FM radio station\"],\n            [\"Radio City\", \"started on\", \"3 July 2001\"],\n            [\"Radio City\", \"plays songs in\", \"Hindi\"],\n            [\"Radio City\", \"plays songs in\", \"English\"],\n            [\"Radio City\", \"forayed into\", \"New Media\"],\n            [\"Radio City\", \"launched\", \"PlanetRadiocity.com\"],\n            [\"PlanetRadiocity.com\", \"launched in\", \"May 2008\"],\n            [\"PlanetRadiocity.com\", \"is\", \"music portal\"],\n            [\"PlanetRadiocity.com\", \"offers\", \"news\"],\n            [\"PlanetRadiocity.com\", \"offers\", \"videos\"],\n            [\"PlanetRadiocity.com\", \"offers\", \"songs\"]\n    ]\n}\n"
 },
 {
  "role": "user",
  "content": "Convert the paragraph into a JSON dict, it has a named entity list and a triple list.\nParagraph:\n```\n${passage}\n```\n\n${named_entity_json}\n"
 }
]
````

</details>

- 결과(`openie_results_qwen3vl-8b.json`): 캡션 226개, 개체 1,990개, triple 2,704개(전처리 로그의 `Total unique entities extracted: 1990`, `Total triples extracted: 2704`와 같음). [확인]
- **triple이 0개인 캡션 18개** [확인]
  - 2개: NER은 됐지만 triple 추출이 3회 모두 실패(로그 `Exception for chunk … RetryError`). 이 단계 로그의 triple 형식 오류는 모두 "triple 원소가 문자열이 아님" 유형이다(int 90건, NoneType 46건, bool 34건; 재시도 중 성공한 호출 포함, 두 캡션과의 짝은 로그로 알 수 없음).
  - 16개: NER 결과부터 빈 목록이다. 로그에 이 캡션들에 대한 오류가 없다 → 모델이 빈 목록을 낸 것으로 보이나 응답 원문이 기록되지 않아 이유는 확인할 수 없다. [부분 확인]
  - 결과: 이 캡션들은 10sec 그래프에서 개체와 연결되지 않은 passage 노드가 된다(dense 유사도로만 검색됨). 캡션 내용 자체는 정상이다.

**HippoRAG 그래프 구성 규칙** (`hipporag/HippoRAG.py`, 기본 설정) [확인]

- 노드: passage(캡션 1개 = 1노드, id `chunk-<md5>`) + entity(triple 주어·목적어, 소문자화 등 정규화 후, id `entity-<md5>`).
- 엣지: ① fact 엣지 = triple 하나마다 주어↔목적어(양방향, 가중치는 등장 횟수) ② passage↔entity 엣지(가중치 1) ③ synonym 엣지 = entity 임베딩 cosine ≥ 0.8인 쌍(가중치 = cosine, 영문·숫자 3자 이하 entity 제외).
- 임베딩: Qwen3-Embedding-4B, 2,560차원. 검색 설정: `linking_top_k` 5, `passage_node_weight` 0.05, PPR damping 0.5.

| 단위 | passage | entity | 빈 문자열 entity | 빈 문자열이 든 triple(OpenIE) | fact(고유 triple) | fact 엣지 | synonym 엣지 | passage–entity 엣지 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10sec | 226 | 1,051 | 1 | 51 | 2,194 | 3,560 | 3,682 | 3,354 |
| 30sec | 76 | 1,033 | 1 | 38 | 1,598 | 2,876 | 3,032 | 1,980 |
| 3min | 13 | 468 | 0 | 0 | 448 | 870 | 629 | 561 |
| 10min | 4 | 320 | 1 | 10 | 299 | 560 | 369 | 353 |
- 엣지 수는 igraph 엣지 수 그대로다(fact·synonym 엣지는 같은 쌍이 두 방향으로 각각 들어 있음).
- "빈 문자열 entity": 주어나 목적어가 빈 문자열인 triple에서 생긴 노드다(HippoRAG는 빈 문자열도 entity로 만든다). [확인]

**예: 10sec 그래프에서 entity `sports dribble specs` 노드의 이웃** (graph.pickle 원본)

- passage 이웃 2개(이 개체가 triple에 나온 10sec 캡션): 00:00:30, 00:00:40
- fact 이웃 3개: `a person`, `close up`, `packaging`
- synonym 이웃 10개(cosine): `dribbling`(0.856), `basketball dribbling challenge`(0.848), `dribbler`(0.842), `dribble time trial`(0.833), `each dribble`(0.832), `dribbling challenge`(0.829), `block dribbler`(0.823), `shoot or dribble`(0.822), `dribble stick`(0.813), `dribbling maneuvers`(0.802)
- (igraph에는 같은 쌍의 엣지가 두 방향으로 각각 들어 있어, 이 노드에 붙은 엣지 수는 passage 2 / fact 6 / synonym 20개다.)
- 검색 때 질의와 비슷한 fact가 이 개체를 가리키면, PPR이 이 엣지들을 따라 위 passage들(과 synonym으로 이어진 개체의 passage)에 점수를 준다.

**synonym 엣지 예: 10sec 그래프에서 cosine이 가장 낮은(0.8에 가까운) 8쌍** (고유 쌍 1,856개 = igraph synonym 엣지 3,682개) — 같은 뜻이 아닌 개체도 이어지는 사례

### 10.5 semantic memory: 추출 → 통합 → 검색에 쓰이는 153개

**① 추출** (`preprocess/semantic_memory/extract_semantic_triples.py`, `memory/semantic/semantic_extraction.py`) [확인]

- 10sec 캡션을 순서대로 **10개씩 묶어**(23묶음), 묶음의 10sec OpenIE triple을 모두 이어 `"<번호>. [주어, 술어, 목적어]"` 목록으로 LLM에 준다. 묶음 키 = `date` 숫자 + 묶음 마지막 캡션의 `end_time`.
- LLM은 `semantic_triples`와 각 triple의 근거 번호 `episodic_evidence`를 JSON으로 낸다. **저장할 때 `episodic_evidence`는 버린다**(코드에서 주석 처리). 그래서 semantic triple에는 시간·근거 연결이 없다.
- 최대 출력 2,048토큰, 3회 재시도 후 실패하면 그 묶음은 빈 목록이 된다.

<details><summary>semantic 추출 프롬프트 원문 (system + one-shot + 입력)</summary>

```
[
 {
  "role": "system",
  "content": "You are tasked with extracting semantic knowledge from episodic triples. \nYour goal is to infer generalizable information that extends beyond the specific episode. \nFocus on capturing valid semantic triples that can guide reasoning about behavior, relationships, or preferences.\n\n# What to Extract:\n1. **Relationships**: social bonds or roles between entities  that persist over time\n   (e.g., \"Alice is a friend with Bob\", \"Jason is a teacher of Alice\").\n2. **Attributes & Preferences**: tendencies, likes/dislikes, personality-like traits, or behavioral habits\n   (e.g., \"Alice prefers not having dessert\", \"Bob enjoys music\").\n3. **Habits & Capabilities**: actions or patterns that suggest what an entity often does, can do, or tends to do\n   (e.g., \"Alice often helps friends\", \"Jason can give advice\").\n4. **Conceptual Knowledge**: directly useful facts that support reasoning, but avoid overly broad taxonomic statements\n   (e.g., \"Alice's office is near Cafe X\", \"Bob's gym is closed on Sundays\").\n\n# What to Avoid:\n- **One-off events or transient states** (e.g., “ate pizza yesterday”, “was late once”) unless explicitly declared as a preference/role\n- **Broad taxonomy or trivia unrelated to behavior** (e.g., “a laptop is electronics”, “Paris is in France”)\n- **Speculative or mind-reading inferences without textual support** (e.g., motives, beliefs not evidenced)\n\n# Important Notes:\n- Prefer to base semantic triples on multiple supporting episodes. \n- BUT if a single episode clearly reflects a role, preference, habit, or capability, it is valid to include it.\n- Each semantic triple MUST have at least one supporting episodic triple.\n- Reduce duplication. If multiple episodic triples support the same or very similar semantic knowledge, merge them into one semantic triple rather than repeating.\n- The `episodic_evidence[i]` list must always point to the indices that support `semantic_triples[i]`.\n- Aim for broad coverage: extract as many valid semantic triples as reasonably supported by the input.\n\n# Output Format:\nReturn ONLY a JSON object with the following two keys:\n- `semantic_triples` (List[List[str]]): Each item is a triple [subject, predicate, object].\n- `episodic_evidence` (List[List[int]]) : Each item is a list of **0-based** indices pointing to the input episodic triples \n   that support the corresponding semantic triple at the same position.\n- The two lists MUST have the same length and aligned order.\n- If no semantic knowledge is inferable, return:\n  {\"semantic_triples\": [], \"episodic_evidence\": []}\n"
 },
 {
  "role": "user",
  "content": "Episodic triples:\n0. [\"Alice\", \"talks to\", \"Bob\"],\n1. [\"Alice\", \"laughs with\", \"Bob\"],\n2. [\"Alice\", \"doesn't eat cake\", \"at restaurant\"],\n3. [\"Alice\", \"shares personal stories with\", \"Bob\"],\n4. [\"Alice\", \"brings coffee to\", \"Bob\"],\n5. [\"Jason\", \"talks to\", \"Alice\"],\n6. [\"Alice\", \"declines dessert\", \"at friend's house\"]\n"
 },
 {
  "role": "assistant",
  "content": "{\n  \"semantic_triples\": [\n    [\"Alice\", \"is a friend with\", \"Bob\"],\n    [\"Alice\", \"prefers\", \"not having dessert\"]\n  ],\n  \"episodic_evidence\": [\n    [0, 1, 3],\n    [2, 6]\n  ]\n}\n"
 },
 {
  "role": "user",
  "content": "Episodic triples:\n${episodic_triples}"
 }
]
```

</details>

- **결과: 23묶음 중 11묶음이 0개**, 나머지 12묶음에서 482개. [확인]
  - 전처리 로그의 semantic 추출 RetryError가 11건으로 0개 묶음 수와 같다. 실패한 묶음만 0개가 되므로 0개 묶음 = 실패 묶음이다.
  - 로그에 남은 파싱 실패 응답 원문 36건 중 35건이 2,047–2,048토큰에서 끊긴 JSON이다(최대 출력 2,048토큰). 25건은 `episodic_evidence` 목록을 쓰다가 끊겼다. → 출력 상한에 걸려 JSON이 완성되지 못한 것이 주원인. [측정]

**② 통합** (`consolidate_semantic_memory.py`, `semantic_consolidation.py`) [확인]

- 묶음 키 순서대로 누적한다. 새 triple마다 기존 누적 triple과 임베딩 cosine을 계산해 **0.6 이상인 것(최대 20개)** 이 있으면 LLM에 "새 triple + 관련 기존 triple"을 주고, ① 새 triple을 어떻게 고칠지 ② 기존 것 중 무엇을 지울지를 받는다. 관련 기존 triple이 없으면 그대로 추가한다.
- 각 시점의 누적 결과 전체를 저장한다(`semantic_consolidation_results_qwen3vl-8b.json`, 23개 키).

**예: 시점 `100282000`의 통합** (지워진 기존 triple이 가장 많은 시점: 54개)

- 이 시점 새 triple 66개 중 LLM이 고친 것 21개. 앞 8개(추출 원문 → 통합 후):
  - `('man', 'takes shot', 'toward hoop')` → `('man', 'shoots', 'basketball')`
  - `('man', 'watches', 'ball go through hoop')` → `('man', 'watches', 'basketball go through hoop')`
  - `('man', 'takes second shot', 'toward hoop')` → `('man', 'shoots', 'basketball toward hoop')`
  - `('man', 'faces', 'man in black t-shirt')` → `('man', 'wears', 'black t-shirt')`
  - `('man in black t-shirt', 'stands with', 'hands on hips')` → `('man in black t-shirt', 'stands with hands on hips', '')`
  - `('other people', 'are visible on', 'outdoor court')` → `('other people', 'are visible', 'on outdoor basketball court')`
  - `('third man', 'is sitting on', 'basketball court')` → `('third man', 'is sitting on', 'outdoor basketball court')`
  - `('scene', 'is on', 'sunny day')` → `('Scene', 'is set under', 'sunny sky')`
- 지워진 기존 triple 앞 8개: `('challenge', 'requires', 'three shots with flick glove')`; `('challenge', 'requires', 'three shots without flick glove')`; `('on-screen graphics', 'increase in number', 'with each successful shot')`; `('on-screen text', 'appears', 'when ball goes in')`; `('man in center', 'is wearing', 'patterned shorts')`; `('man on left', 'wears', "red and white 'ZHYPE' jersey")`; `('man on left', 'wears', "red and white 'ZHYPE' jersey")`; `('man on the left', 'takes drink from', 'water bottle')`
- 지운 이유(LLM 응답)는 기록되지 않는다. 위 짝은 파일 비교로만 얻은 것이다. [확인]

**③ 검색에 쓰이는 semantic memory** — `query_time` 123595999 이하의 마지막 시점 `100373700`의 누적 153개만 쓴다(`SemanticMemory.index`). 검색 서비스 로그 `semantic 153`과 같다. [확인]

- 개체 그래프: 개체(주어·목적어, 빈 문자열 제외) 172개, 엣지 150개(주어≠목적어인 triple). 목적어가 빈 triple 1개.
- 검색(`SemanticMemory.retrieve`, top_k = `semantic_k_per_query` 5): 질의 임베딩과 cosine 상위 5개 triple → 그 triple들의 개체를 출발점으로 PPR(damping 0.85) → triple 점수 = 주어 PPR + 목적어 PPR → 상위 5개. 질의 여러 개의 목록을 RRF(k=60)로 합쳐 `semantic_k` 4개를 writer에 준다.
- 연결이 많은 개체 상위 10: `player`(20), `man`(19), `basketball court`(9), `basketball`(7), `third man`(6), `commentary`(5), `camera`(5), `man on the right`(5), `Flick Gloves`(5), `black hoodie`(5)

### 10.6 visual memory: 10sec 구간마다 VLM2Vec 비디오 임베딩 1개

- 파일 `visual_embeddings.pkl`: dict, 키 = 10sec `start_time`(226개), 값 = numpy float32 벡터 (1536,). [확인]
- 프레임 수 확인: 저장된 임베딩을 CPU에서 10장·16장(WorldMM 기본값)으로 다시 만들어 비교했다(`analysis/verify_visual_nframes.py`). cosine은 00:00:40 10장 0.9987 / 16장 0.91058; 00:34:40 10장 0.99829 / 16장 0.8867; 00:28:50 10장 0.99868 / 16장 0.94282; 00:18:20 10장 0.99654 / 16장 0.95321 → **10장**으로 만든 것이다. [확인]
- 입력 프레임: 구간마다 **10장**(`--num-frames 10`). 시작 프레임 = ⌈시작초 × fps⌉, 끝 프레임 = ⌊끝초 × fps⌋, 그 사이를 `linspace(시작, 끝, 10)` 반올림. 디코더는 전처리 당시 `torchcodec`(로그). 프레임 범위는 로그 226줄과 코드 재계산이 모두 같다. [확인]
- 크기: 프레임당 최대 360×420 = 151,200픽셀 제한으로 1280×720 → **504×280**(28의 배수, `smart_resize`). 텍스트 지시문 `Represent the given video.`와 함께 임베딩. [확인]
- 캡션용 프레임(§10.2, 매 정수 초)과 visual 임베딩용 프레임(균등 10장)은 **서로 다른 프레임**이다. 아래 그림의 프레임 번호를 비교하면 보인다.

**구간 00:00:40 — VLM2Vec 입력 10장** (프레임 960–1198 → 960, 986, 1013, 1039, 1066, 1092, 1119, 1145, 1172, 1198)

- 검색 때: image query를 VLM2Vec 텍스트 인코더로 임베딩 → 226개 구간 임베딩과 cosine → 상위 3구간 → 구간 **중앙 시각**의 프레임 1장을 잘라 writer에 캡션과 함께 넘긴다(§10.7).

### 10.9 섹션별 모듈 입력·출력 전부

<a id="s10-9-0"></a>

#### 10.9.0 검색 재현 방법과 일치 확인

- 실행 기록에는 질의 × 단위별 그래프 검색 결과, RRF 후보 목록, L1 필터 프롬프트가 없다. 그래서 `analysis/reproduce_retrieval_cpu.py`가 **검색 서비스의 `WorldMMRetriever` 클래스 그대로**, HippoRAG 캐시의 **복사본**으로, 임베딩 모델만 CPU(sdpa)에서 돌렸다. LLM은 호출하지 않는다(L1 필터 응답은 재현할 수 없음).
- 실행 당시에는 GPU(flash_attention_2)였다. 그래서 섹션마다 아래를 실행 기록과 맞춰 보고, **맞은 항목만 그 섹션의 내부 과정으로 싣는다.** 맞지 않은 항목은 "재현 불가"로 표시하고, 기록에 남은 사실(선택된 근거·점수)과 어긋난 지점만 보인다. [확인]
  - text: RRF 후보 수 = 검색 서비스 로그 `episodic_candidates` · 기록된 episodic 근거 8개가 재현 후보에 있고 RRF 점수(소수 6자리)가 같음 · 다시 만든 L1 필터 프롬프트의 토큰 수(서버와 같은 계산법) = LLM 서버 로그
  - semantic: 근거 4개의 id·순서·점수가 같음
  - image: 근거 3개의 구간·순서가 같음
  - 실제 캐시는 실행 전후 md5가 같다(`eba672f239fb719ff11aa391d48fc84d`).
- 설정: 질의당 후보 {"10sec": 3, "30sec": 3, "3min": 2, "10min": 1}, RRF k=60, HippoRAG `linking_top_k` 5, semantic 질의당 5개, visual 질의당 3개. 텍스트 임베딩 `Qwen3-Embedding-4B CPU bf16 sdpa`.
- HippoRAG 점수는 PPR 점수(그래프 경로) 또는 dense 유사도(fact가 없을 때)라 단위끼리 비교할 수 없다. 그래서 서비스는 점수 대신 순위로 RRF를 한다.
- **일치 판정의 한계**: 실행 기록에서 직접 맞춰 볼 수 있는 것은 위 값들뿐이다. text가 "일치"인 섹션의 고르지 않은 후보는 "후보 수 + L1 프롬프트 토큰 수(후보 텍스트 전체가 들어감)"가 같다는 것으로만 확인된다. 텍스트가 다른데 토큰 수만 우연히 같을 가능성까지 배제하지는 못한다. 또 RRF 점수가 같은 후보끼리의 순서(표의 순위, 재구성한 L1 프롬프트 안의 후보 순서)는 기록과 대조할 수 없다. [부분 확인]

| 섹션 | RRF 후보 수 (재현 / 기록) | episodic 점수 불일치 | L1 프롬프트 토큰 (재현 / 기록) | semantic | image | 이 문서에 싣는 재현 결과 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | 16 / 17 | 2개 | 8389 / 8661 | 일치 | 일치 | semantic, image |
| S2 | 22 / 22 | 1개 | 9020 / 9055 | 일치 | 일치 | semantic, image |
| S3 | 17 / 17 | 0개 | 9058 / 9058 | **불일치** | 일치 | text, image |
| S4 | 25 / 25 | 0개 | 10737 / 10709 | 일치 | 일치 | semantic, image |
| S5 | 22 / 22 | 0개 | 9288 / 9288 | 일치 | 일치 | text, semantic, image |
| S6 | 26 / 26 | 0개 | 12112 / 12112 | **불일치** | 일치 | text, image |

- 맞은 섹션: text S3, S5, S6 / semantic S1, S2, S4, S5 / image S1, S2, S3, S4, S5, S6.
- text가 어긋난 섹션: 기록된 근거의 RRF 점수가 다른 섹션(S1, S2)은 그 근거가 목록 하나에 더 들어가거나 빠지거나 순위가 한 칸 바뀐 값이다(각 섹션 ③의 근거). 점수는 모두 같은데 L1 프롬프트 토큰 수만 다른 섹션(S4)은 L1이 고르지 않은 후보 일부가 다르다. 모두 목록 **끝자리 근처의 순위 차이**다. [확인]
- 원인: 섹션 1·2를 CPU에서 float32와 bfloat16으로 따로 돌려 본 진단에서 text 후보는 두 정밀도가 서로 같았고, 둘 다 기록과 같은 지점에서 달랐다. 그래서 CPU와 GPU(flash_attention_2) 사이 질의 임베딩의 미세한 차이로 보인다. GPU로 다시 돌려 확인하지는 않았다. [부분 확인]
- 재현의 실행 간 차이: 이 표는 2026-11-02 CPU 재현 결과다. 2026-11-10에 같은 코드·같은 데이터(캐시 md5 동일)로 다시 돌린 두 번의 결과는 서로도, 이 표와도 달랐다(예: S1 text — 11-02 불일치, 11-10 한 번은 일치·한 번은 불일치). CPU 재현 자체가 실행마다 점수가 조금씩 달라(그래프 검색 점수 최대 차이 약 0.008) 점수가 비슷한 후보의 순위가 바뀐다. 그래서 "맞은 섹션" 목록은 고정된 값이 아니다. [확인: 대조 실험, `internal/status/REORG_LOG_20261110.md` 9절] 실행마다 달라지는 구체적 기제는 확인하지 않았다. [가설]

## How to read the evidence
- Text sources starting with "[HH:MM:SS-HH:MM:SS | episodic <scale>]" describe that part of the video (built from its frames and speech). Scales 10sec and 30sec give fine details; 3min and 10min are summaries of longer spans.
- Text sources starting with "[video-level knowledge | semantic]" are facts inferred from the whole video, written as (subject, predicate, object). They have NO timestamp.
- Image sources "[Source imgN: [HH:MM:SS-HH:MM:SS | video frame at Xs] description]" are frames taken from the video at that moment, with a description of that moment.

# Grounding Rules (CRITICAL)
1. State only what the evidence supports. Do not add outside knowledge, assumptions, or speculation about intentions or feelings unless the evidence states them.
2. When describing an event, give its time from the evidence in HH:MM:SS form (e.g., "At 00:12:40, ..."). Never invent or estimate times that are not in the evidence. Do not attach times to video-level knowledge.
3. If sources conflict, prefer the finer-scale (10sec/30sec) description and mention the uncertainty.
4. If the evidence does not cover a requirement, say briefly that the retrieved footage does not show it instead of filling the gap. If no evidence was retrieved at all, write a short section that says so.
5. Describe events in chronological order unless the section needs another structure.
6. Do not repeat a fact, sentence, or paragraph you have already written in this section. If a fact was already covered in a previous section (see "Context from Previous Sections"), mention it in at most one short sentence and focus on what is new in this section. Exception: a conclusion section (see "Conclusion Section") restates earlier results briefly by design.
7. Each text source covers only its own time span. Words such as "the video opens", "begins", "closes", "ends" or "concludes" inside a 30sec, 3min or 10min summary refer to the start or end of THAT span, not of the whole video. The whole video runs from 00:00:00 to 00:37:37. Describe how the whole video begins or ends only with sources whose time range reaches its first or last minutes; otherwise do not claim how the video begins or ends.

# Citation Rules (CRITICAL)
1. Text citation: put [citation:txt1], [citation:txt2], ... at the end of each sentence or claim that uses a text source. Every factual sentence needs at least one citation.
2. Image citation: to show a frame, put ![](citation:img1), ![](citation:img2), ... on its own line right after the sentence describing that moment. Use only sources marked as images, and include the 1-3 most relevant frames when available.
3. Use exactly these formats with one source per bracket; for several sources write [citation:txt1][citation:txt3].
4. Never write [citation:imgN]: an image source is cited ONLY as ![](citation:imgN) on its own line, and [citation:...] is used ONLY for txt sources.

# Position-Aware Writing Instructions
**Is this the FIRST section?** yes
**Is this the LAST section?** no
- FIRST section: open by introducing the video and what the report covers; do not conclude the report.
- MIDDLE section: start with a smooth transition; do not use concluding phrases such as "In conclusion", "To summarize", or "Overall, this report".
- LAST section: you may synthesize the main points of the whole report, using only evidence-supported statements.

## How to read the evidence
- Text sources starting with "[HH:MM:SS-HH:MM:SS | episodic <scale>]" describe that part of the video (built from its frames and speech). Scales 10sec and 30sec give fine details; 3min and 10min are summaries of longer spans.
- Text sources starting with "[video-level knowledge | semantic]" are facts inferred from the whole video, written as (subject, predicate, object). They have NO timestamp.
- Image sources "[Source imgN: [HH:MM:SS-HH:MM:SS | video frame at Xs] description]" are frames taken from the video at that moment, with a description of that moment.

# Grounding Rules (CRITICAL)
1. State only what the evidence supports. Do not add outside knowledge, assumptions, or speculation about intentions or feelings unless the evidence states them.
2. When describing an event, give its time from the evidence in HH:MM:SS form (e.g., "At 00:12:40, ..."). Never invent or estimate times that are not in the evidence. Do not attach times to video-level knowledge.
3. If sources conflict, prefer the finer-scale (10sec/30sec) description and mention the uncertainty.
4. If the evidence does not cover a requirement, say briefly that the retrieved footage does not show it instead of filling the gap. If no evidence was retrieved at all, write a short section that says so.
5. Describe events in chronological order unless the section needs another structure.
6. Do not repeat a fact, sentence, or paragraph you have already written in this section. If a fact was already covered in a previous section (see "Context from Previous Sections"), mention it in at most one short sentence and focus on what is new in this section. Exception: a conclusion section (see "Conclusion Section") restates earlier results briefly by design.
7. Each text source covers only its own time span. Words such as "the video opens", "begins", "closes", "ends" or "concludes" inside a 30sec, 3min or 10min summary refer to the start or end of THAT span, not of the whole video. The whole video runs from 00:00:00 to 00:37:37. Describe how the whole video begins or ends only with sources whose time range reaches its first or last minutes; otherwise do not claim how the video begins or ends.

# Citation Rules (CRITICAL)
1. Text citation: put [citation:txt1], [citation:txt2], ... at the end of each sentence or claim that uses a text source. Every factual sentence needs at least one citation.
2. Image citation: to show a frame, put ![](citation:img1), ![](citation:img2), ... on its own line right after the sentence describing that moment. Use only sources marked as images, and include the 1-3 most relevant frames when available.
3. Use exactly these formats with one source per bracket; for several sources write [citation:txt1][citation:txt3].
4. Never write [citation:imgN]: an image source is cited ONLY as ![](citation:imgN) on its own line, and [citation:...] is used ONLY for txt sources.

# Position-Aware Writing Instructions
**Is this the FIRST section?** no
**Is this the LAST section?** no
- FIRST section: open by introducing the video and what the report covers; do not conclude the report.
- MIDDLE section: start with a smooth transition; do not use concluding phrases such as "In conclusion", "To summarize", or "Overall, this report".
- LAST section: you may synthesize the main points of the whole report, using only evidence-supported statements.

# Conclusion Section
If the Section Description starts with "Conclusion:", write a brief conclusion of 100-250 words: summarize only the main results already covered by the previous sections and answer the report topic at a high level. Do not introduce new events or details, keep at most one short paragraph per checklist item, and still cite the evidence above for every factual statement. If you state how the video ends, follow Grounding Rule 7.

# Format
- Start with a section title written as "# Title"; use "##" for subsections if needed.
- Typically 250-700 words, depending on how much evidence is available (a conclusion section: 100-250 words).
- Output ONLY the section content, without meta-commentary.

## How to read the evidence
- Text sources starting with "[HH:MM:SS-HH:MM:SS | episodic <scale>]" describe that part of the video (built from its frames and speech). Scales 10sec and 30sec give fine details; 3min and 10min are summaries of longer spans.
- Text sources starting with "[video-level knowledge | semantic]" are facts inferred from the whole video, written as (subject, predicate, object). They have NO timestamp.
- Image sources "[Source imgN: [HH:MM:SS-HH:MM:SS | video frame at Xs] description]" are frames taken from the video at that moment, with a description of that moment.

# Grounding Rules (CRITICAL)
1. State only what the evidence supports. Do not add outside knowledge, assumptions, or speculation about intentions or feelings unless the evidence states them.
2. When describing an event, give its time from the evidence in HH:MM:SS form (e.g., "At 00:12:40, ..."). Never invent or estimate times that are not in the evidence. Do not attach times to video-level knowledge.
3. If sources conflict, prefer the finer-scale (10sec/30sec) description and mention the uncertainty.
4. If the evidence does not cover a requirement, say briefly that the retrieved footage does not show it instead of filling the gap. If no evidence was retrieved at all, write a short section that says so.
5. Describe events in chronological order unless the section needs another structure.
6. Do not repeat a fact, sentence, or paragraph you have already written in this section. If a fact was already covered in a previous section (see "Context from Previous Sections"), mention it in at most one short sentence and focus on what is new in this section. Exception: a conclusion section (see "Conclusion Section") restates earlier results briefly by design.
7. Each text source covers only its own time span. Words such as "the video opens", "begins", "closes", "ends" or "concludes" inside a 30sec, 3min or 10min summary refer to the start or end of THAT span, not of the whole video. The whole video runs from 00:00:00 to 00:37:37. Describe how the whole video begins or ends only with sources whose time range reaches its first or last minutes; otherwise do not claim how the video begins or ends.

# Citation Rules (CRITICAL)
1. Text citation: put [citation:txt1], [citation:txt2], ... at the end of each sentence or claim that uses a text source. Every factual sentence needs at least one citation.
2. Image citation: to show a frame, put ![](citation:img1), ![](citation:img2), ... on its own line right after the sentence describing that moment. Use only sources marked as images, and include the 1-3 most relevant frames when available.
3. Use exactly these formats with one source per bracket; for several sources write [citation:txt1][citation:txt3].
4. Never write [citation:imgN]: an image source is cited ONLY as ![](citation:imgN) on its own line, and [citation:...] is used ONLY for txt sources.

# Position-Aware Writing Instructions
**Is this the FIRST section?** no
**Is this the LAST section?** no
- FIRST section: open by introducing the video and what the report covers; do not conclude the report.
- MIDDLE section: start with a smooth transition; do not use concluding phrases such as "In conclusion", "To summarize", or "Overall, this report".
- LAST section: you may synthesize the main points of the whole report, using only evidence-supported statements.

# Conclusion Section
If the Section Description starts with "Conclusion:", write a brief conclusion of 100-250 words: summarize only the main results already covered by the previous sections and answer the report topic at a high level. Do not introduce new events or details, keep at most one short paragraph per checklist item, and still cite the evidence above for every factual statement. If you state how the video ends, follow Grounding Rule 7.

# Format
- Start with a section title written as "# Title"; use "##" for subsections if needed.
- Typically 250-700 words, depending on how much evidence is available (a conclusion section: 100-250 words).
- Output ONLY the section content, without meta-commentary.

1. State only what the evidence supports. Do not add outside knowledge, assumptions, or speculation about intentions or feelings unless the evidence states them.
2. When describing an event, give its time from the evidence in HH:MM:SS form (e.g., "At 00:12:40, ..."). Never invent or estimate times that are not in the evidence. Do not attach times to video-level knowledge.

Words such as "the video opens", "begins", "closes", "ends" or "concludes" inside a 30sec, 3min or 10min summary refer to the start or end of THAT span, not of the whole video. The whole video runs from 00:00:00 to 00:37:37. Describe how the whole video begins or ends only with sources whose time range reaches its first or last minutes; otherwise do not claim how the video begins or ends.

# Citation Rules (CRITICAL)
1. Text citation: put [citation:txt1], [citation:txt2], ... at the end of each sentence or claim that uses a text source. Every factual sentence needs at least one citation.
2. Image citation: to show a frame, put ![](citation:img1), ![](citation:img2), ... on its own line right after the sentence describing that moment. Use only sources marked as images, and include the 1-3 most relevant frames when available.
3. Use exactly these formats with one source per bracket; for several sources write [citation:txt1][citation:txt3].
4. Never write [citation:imgN]: an image source is cited ONLY as ![](citation:imgN) on its own line, and [citation:...] is used ONLY for txt sources.

# Position-Aware Writing Instructions
**Is this the FIRST section?** no
**Is this the LAST section?** yes
- FIRST section: open by introducing the video and what the report covers; do not conclude the report.
- MIDDLE section: start with a smooth transition; do not use concluding phrases such as "In conclusion", "To summarize", or "Overall, this report".
- LAST section: you may synthesize the main points of the whole report, using only evidence-supported statements.

Do not introduce new events or details, keep at most one short paragraph per checklist item, and still cite the evidence above for every factual statement. If you state how the video ends, follow Grounding Rule 7.
